The danger lies

By: Annalise Lubbe | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Behind the posh and glamour of horseracing are the lesser known facts about the riders who steer these thoroughbreds. In Carte Blanche tonight we go behind the scenes to tell the story.

Unique Selling Point:
Behind the posh and glamour of horseracing are the lesser known facts about the riders who steer these thoroughbreds. In tonight’s episode of Carte Blanche we go behind the scenes and into the jockey’s changeroom on racing day, when shedding the last 500gram in the box (sauna) stands between you and being disqualified. When the scale becomes your enemy and your weight the controlling dial the price you pay to stay in the game takes its toll every step of the way.

In the X-games of horses jockeys control half-ton thoroughbreds at neck-breaking speeds, leaving them open to injuries of the worst kind. From broken ribs to collarbones, feet and hands, these are common accidents on the race course every jockey face and those who survive get back into the saddle again.

Stamina, capacity for pain, discipline on diet, a challenging lifestyle not cut out for the faint hearted. Jockeys have to have nerves of steel, make split second decisions and never think about the possibility that the beast they steer could stumble and fall, break its leg, tear a tendon, and all that at 60 kilometres per hour with no breaks to put on.


Summary:
Summary:
We track a legend who have made history, those who are at the top of their game and the newbie’s; fearless and part of a new generation of jockeys who are invited to compete overseas and taking the challenge.

We talk to them and their family about the challenges, their coping mechanisms and how they manage to survive the challenges of weight control, injuries and suspensions - a reality they live with every day.


Further information:
Our story:

Bernard Fayd’Herbe wages a constant battle with the scales, as evidenced by the number of times during an afternoon that the commentator announces “plus a half” as he takes his mount down to the start. When he goes on holiday his weight soars from 57kg to as much as 66 kg – “and even at that I still wouldn’t be completely letting myself go. No burgers or anything like that.” Getting the weight down again involves huge willpower. “I have to lose the weight before I exercise. Once you turn the fat into muscle, it can be very hard to get rid of it.”

Surprisingly his diet includes three meals a day. He has a cup of black coffee when he gets up and he will have another, or some water, when he is riding work. On returning home he makes himself an omelet. Lunch is fish or steak with salad, and dinner is small, perhaps soup. “You can’t starve yourself. You’ve got to keep healthy but I try to stick to less carbs and low protein.”

But the intake has to be paid for and the cost is agonisingly high. He runs a minimum of 10k a day, always in sweat clothes, and on race days he has to sweat again. He reckons a steaming hot bath will shed a kilo and a brisk walk round a racetrack will take off 50% more, assuming the day is sufficiently hot and the clothes heavy enough. At one stage he had to pick and choose his rides on big days because he didn’t have enough energy to ride through the card.

There are up to 8 races on a card during competition days. Most jockeys will push their limit and ride all 8 races to maximise their chances of winning. But dehydration and lack of food takes its toll. Rakeesh Jeewanlall, Stipendiary Steward at the Greyville Race Course checks the status of the jockeys before a race and will pull them off if they look too anemic to compete. “Even a glass of water,” he adds, will add too much weight to the jockey so he has to go through the day without any liquid, or go into the box to sweat it out.

Garth Puller, former legend Cape jockey with an illustrious career in the saddle and two July wins will tell you that he lived off dried fruit and orange juice for many months, constantly starving himself to maintain the required weight of a professional jockey. This places a great deal of pressure on the jockey to maintain a low body weight, in order to attain rides. Unlike other weight category sports, horseracing does not have an off-season, therefore jockeys are constantly pressured to maintain a below normal body weight. This results in dangerous weight control practices and compromised health.

Kathleen Krog, a dietician from Durban recently did a study on apprentice jockeys and found that their micronutrient intakes were 67% below the recommended intake. 91% of the jockeys reported the use of one or more weight control method including skipping meals, excessive exercising to sweat, using the sweatbox (sauna) and in some instances suffering from hunger pains and being over tired. These jockeys are therefore at risk for long-term health consequences including low bone mineral density.

Jockeys weigh between 48 and 57 kilograms. The lighter the jockey, the better the horse performs and the faster it goes. On a racecourse the average speed is 60 kilometers per hour.
The flip side of being a lightweight jockey means very little control over a beast weighing half a ton and literally running at break necking speeds to the winning post.

Justine King has a light frame and is currently the only licensed female jockey in South Africa competes in a male dominant sport. Her life has not been an easy ride and she often have to forfeit a good horse to a male jockey after she has put in the time to train and exercise the animal for a competition. “They just don’t think a girl can do it”, she says. But I am in it and am going to keep on trying to get a win behind my name”. My schooling at the Jockey Academy was tough but the best you can get to get you started,” she exclaims.

Laying the foundation for training is the Jockey academy in Summerveld. At 15 years of age applicants are accepted based on their required weight, height and school marks. After five years of skills and academic training those who pass enter the professional arena. Jockeys typically race until they are well in the fifty’s provided they have not suffered from severe lifelong injuries.

Retired jockey, Garth accounts one of his several injuries were shortly before race day. “I fracture my wrist and asked the doctor to tie it up. I had to race’. Nowadays they are much more strict. The doctor has to sign you as fit to compete.”

Bone fractures and concussion are common injuries. Dr. Jon Patricios, sports physician has treated many jockey injuries at his practice in Johannesburg and found that concussion is often a top cause of falling off the horse at high speeds. The unnatural position of a jockey also accounts for suffering from lower back-pain as thirty one year old Muzi Yeni will tell you. He lives with back pain and is not allowed to take anything stronger than Panado on race days or he will be disqualified.

Winning is what it is all about as jockeys get paid a meager R856.50 per race: hardly enough to get out of bed for. Most jockeys are freelancers and will do as many rides a possible on race days to increase their chances to win. Ten percent is the payout for the winning horse and seven percent if you come second, third or fourth.

When the stakes are high and everybody wants their share of the payout, no stone will be left unturned. Owners or racehorse trainers will be the first to question the results if they think the jockey has failed to steer the horse in a clear winning position. The National Horseracing Authority governs the sport and any irregularities will be investigated. If the organisation finds that the jockey has been at fault a suspension will be given.

South Africa can compete with the best and has produced some of the world’s best jockeys. Anthony Delpech has benefited from gaining international experience and honing his skills in Hong Kong. He has been selected as part of the Rest Of The World Team for the Dubai Duty Free Shergar Cup to be held at Ascot Racecourse in August this year.

Script:


Script: FINAL: The danger lies: 2nd viewing script- APPROVED 20 JUNE 2017

Up audio: bell ringing in jockeys room

V/O. There are 364 race meetings every year in South Africa, at Greyville, Turffontein, Kenilworth, Scottsville, to name but a few of our horseracing tracks. This is where jockeys earn their living. In an industry that turns over R7 billion a year, top jockeys earn millions, but it comes at a cost.

Anthony Delpech: Professional jockey: I miss a lot of my kids growing up especially when they were playing sports or any activity at school. I get to miss out on all of those, all the I am racing but whenever I get half a chance I will be there watching and it is very sad.

V/O At 48 Anthony is at the peak of his career: three-hundred-and-thirty-four wins in one season, four-time winner of the Vodacom Durban July with international experience in places like Hong Kong. He is married to Candice for 24 years but being away so often is tough on the family.

Candice Delpech: The kids really miss anthony when he is not around. He misses out on sporting events and father’s days and matric dances and the school life for the kids.

UP audio: Last word, brightly

Candice Delpech: So I have to be the rock in the family when he isn’t around because he is away long hours at a time. It is difficult. It is like being a single mom sometimes.

Up audio: Anthony on mechanical horse

Candice Delpech: The sacrifice of being a jockey’s wife, your husband races 6 days of the week. You don’t really see him often, he leaves six o’clock in the morning, he probably gets back nine or ten at night then he will still come home, have dinner and go through the replays again, so yeah racing is our life, it’s 24/7, 365 days of the year.

UP audio: early morning training.

V/O For the jockeys, training starts at 6h00 every morning working the horses, honing their skills and getting them race fit. Muzi Yeni is a natural; his small frame and light weight make him ideal for the sport.

Muzi Yeni: Professional jockey: I took on quite well. I was small. It was easy to ride. I did not have problems riding. It all came to me quite easy. I had a lot of help from the riding master.

V/O Muzi’s professional career started ten years ago. At 30 he has won four Grade One Races and has ridden a thousand one hundred winners at the racetrack. Jockeys earn their bread and butter on race days. The more races they do the better their chances of winning. There are few off days in the jockey calendar.

Muzi Yeni: Professional jockey: I race probably five times a week. It is challenging because you are at home and racing, your day starts early. You are meant to be at work before six. You probably leave the track at nine o’clock. From twelve o’clock to five o’clock, racing programme of eight races, sometimes ten races. So doing that five times a week, it is very strenuous.

V/O It is midweek at a race meeting in Greyville, Durban. A set routine plays out from the moment of arrival: get changed, check your weight; go into the steambath to shed the excess weight and on the scale again. Jockeys weigh as little as 47kg and at most 57kg.

Link: Many factors come into play to make sure that each horse has the best possible chance to win. One of the most important however is the jockey’s weight which is very closely monitored. A few hundred grams overweight could compromise the jockey’s opportunity to even ride.

V/O The Stipendiary Steward at Greyville is Rakeesh Jeewanlall. His job is to monitor every aspect of the race that can have an effect on the performance of the horse.

Rakeesh Jeewanlall: Stipendiary Steward - National Horceracing Authority KZN:
Well it is quite critical that a jockey carries the correct weight, has carded for that particular race that he is participating in. If the weight is extra, obviously it will affect the handicap of the horse and it could obviously affects the result or the performance of that horse.

Anthony Delpech: Our life is run by weight because as a jockey you try and ride the lightest weight you can because that means you get more opportunities in the races.

Candice Delpech: On a typical race day he will only have a cup of tea for breakfast and nothing else the whole day till dinnertime.

V/O Kathy Krog, a dietician from Durban, conducted a study in Hillcrest on twenty apprentice jockeys. She found that the micronutrient intake of the majority of jockeys during and after competition days was insufficient.

Kathy Krog: Dietician: With the research I did at the Academy it was almost 91%, already at an apprentice stage are battling with their weight and using some form of weight control method whether it be food restriction, fluid restriction, sweating, extra exercise and that has deteriorating effect on their health long term.

V/O Billy Jacobson, a professional jockey from KwaZulu-Natal has been racing for twelve years and is constantly at war with the scales.

Billy Jacobson: Professional jockey: That’s part of our life in keeping our weight down. For me if I got a light ride coming up I generally won’t eat a day or two before and hot baths and going for a run with sweat clothes on. Putting plastics on, jersey, looking like I am going into the show going for runs like that.

V/O The danger for the jockeys lies in the fact that dieting becomes a way of life. There are no off days because unlike other seasonal sports, horse racing is all year round.

Kathy Krog: With the jockeys they have to do it so regularly that their eating patterns is what we would term disordered.

Up audio: Horses taking off from starting point.

V/O Horse racing is one of the most dangerous sports. Every time a jockey gets into the saddle he takes his life in his own hands.

Muzi Yeni: So we travel between 55 and close to 65 km an hour. The really top top horses can do 55 seconds over a 1000 metres. So they move.

Up audio: Rakeesh in control room rewinding the video on screen and discussing race

Rakeesh Jeewanlall: We have emergency services during each running of the race. They follow the field from start to finish so in the event that a horse is broken down and a jockey is dislodged that paramedics are there immediately and our vet is also following the field there to take care of the horse.

Anthony Delpech: It is a very dangerous sport. I think I have most probably broken every bone in my body; I have broken my legs; both my collarbones, fractured my skull. I have had my fair share of falls in racing but I think in every sports there is your injury but at the speed we are going, 60, 70 k’s per hour, if you fall at that speed you are going to get hurt.

Claire Mawisa: And you still come back for more?

Anthony Delpech: Well you have to come back for more. If you feel nervous I think you must hang up your boots because that’s when you won’t be riding your best. You have to just put it behind you and get on with it otherwise you end up losing your nerve which several jockeys I have seen have lost their nerve.

V/O Dr Jon Patricios is a Sports Physician in Johannesburg and has been treating jockeys with severe injuries for the past 20 years.

Dr Jon Patricios: Sports Physician. Most of the fractures that we see will incur around the shoulder and collarbone area from falls, and similarly we see dislocations in terms of the more severe injuries that is going to cause potential life threatening conditions. Head injuries are top of the list and jockeys suffer more concussions than any other sports.

Muzi Yeni: I had one incident where a horse had a heart attack at Greyville. A horse had a heart attack in the middle of a pack but I was fortunate, I only suffered concussion. But I have been fortunate I haven’t broken bones like my colleagues have but a lot of concussion.

V/O Concussion accounts for about 20% of jockey injuries; fractures and dislocations another 20% each and less severe injuries the remaining 40%.

Dr. Jon Patricios: The difficulty with concussion is there is no visible wound. A jockey who has a headache, has blurred vision, can’t concentrate and has poor balance is a risk to himself and to others.

Candice: Delpech: It’s really scary with Anthony out there riding. I only watch him in a race just to make sure he crosses the line safe and sound.

Audio up: Anthony at winning post

V/O Tonight’s race at the Greyville racecourse ends on a high note for Anthony as he safely crosses the finishing line in first place.

Claire Mawisa: Congratulations on your win! Is it still a thrill?

Anthony Delpech: Every winner is a thrill. Obviously the bigger ones is more of a thrill but every winner, it is difficult to have a winner, so it is a thrill.

V/O The pressure of winning takes its toll on every jockey. The highs and the lows are there every day as they compete in a sport that takes no prisoners.

Muzi Yeni: On the race track whether you break a bone or whatever happens you have to be able to get back on that horse the next day because it is your livelihood it is your bread and butter. You got to be able to take the bull by its horns.

Anthony Delpech: Professional jockey: I miss a lot of my kids growing up especially when they were playing sports or any activity at school. I get to miss out on all of those, all the I am racing but whenever I get half a chance I will be there watching and it is very sad. V/O At 48 Anthony is at the peak of his career: three-hundred-and-thirty-four wins in one season, four-time winner of the Vodacom Durban July with international experience in places like Hong Kong. He is married to Candice for 24 years but being away so often is tough on the family. Candice Delpech: The kids really miss anthony when he is not around. He misses out on sporting events and father’s days and matric dances and the school life for the kids. UP audio: Last word, brightly Candice Delpech: So I have to be the rock in the family when he isn’t around because he is away long hours at a time. It is difficult. It is like being a single mom sometimes. Up audio: Anthony on mechanical horse Candice Delpech: The sacrifice of being a jockey’s wife, your husband races 6 days of the week. You don’t really see him often, he leaves six o’clock in the morning, he probably gets back nine or ten at night then he will still come home, have dinner and go through the replays again, so yeah racing is our life, it’s 24/7, 365 days of the year. UP audio: early morning training. V/O For the jockeys, training starts at 6h00 every morning working the horses, honing their skills and getting them race fit. Muzi Yeni is a natural; his small frame and light weight make him ideal for the sport. Muzi Yeni: Professional jockey: I took on quite well. I was small. It was easy to ride. I did not have problems riding. It all came to me quite easy. I had a lot of help from the riding master. V/O Muzi’s professional career started ten years ago. At 30 he has won four Grade One Races and has ridden a thousand one hundred winners at the racetrack. Jockeys earn their bread and butter on race days. The more races they do the better their chances of winning. There are few off days in the jockey calendar. Muzi Yeni: Professional jockey: I race probably five times a week. It is challenging because you are at home and racing, your day starts early. You are meant to be at work before six. You probably leave the track at nine o’clock. From twelve o’clock to five o’clock, racing programme of eight races, sometimes ten races. So doing that five times a week, it is very strenuous. V/O It is midweek at a race meeting in Greyville, Durban. A set routine plays out from the moment of arrival: get changed, check your weight; go into the steambath to shed the excess weight and on the scale again. Jockeys weigh as little as 47kg and at most 57kg. Link: Many factors come into play to make sure that each horse has the best possible chance to win. One of the most important however is the jockey’s weight which is very closely monitored. A few hundred grams overweight could compromise the jockey’s opportunity to even ride. V/O The Stipendiary Steward at Greyville is Rakeesh Jeewanlall. His job is to monitor every aspect of the race that can have an effect on the performance of the horse. Rakeesh Jeewanlall: Stipendiary Steward - National Horceracing Authority KZN: Well it is quite critical that a jockey carries the correct weight, has carded for that particular race that he is participating in. If the weight is extra, obviously it will affect the handicap of the horse and it could obviously affects the result or the performance of that horse. Anthony Delpech: Our life is run by weight because as a jockey you try and ride the lightest weight you can because that means you get more opportunities in the races. Candice Delpech: On a typical race day he will only have a cup of tea for breakfast and nothing else the whole day till dinnertime. V/O Kathy Krog, a dietician from Durban, conducted a study in Hillcrest on twenty apprentice jockeys. She found that the micronutrient intake of the majority of jockeys during and after competition days was insufficient. Kathy Krog: Dietician: With the research I did at the Academy it was almost 91%, already at an apprentice stage are battling with their weight and using some form of weight control method whether it be food restriction, fluid restriction, sweating, extra exercise and that has deteriorating effect on their health long term. V/O Billy Jacobson, a professional jockey from KwaZulu-Natal has been racing for twelve years and is constantly at war with the scales. Billy Jacobson: Professional jockey: That’s part of our life in keeping our weight down. For me if I got a light ride coming up I generally won’t eat a day or two before and hot baths and going for a run with sweat clothes on. Putting plastics on, jersey, looking like I am going into the show going for runs like that. V/O The danger for the jockeys lies in the fact that dieting becomes a way of life. There are no off days because unlike other seasonal sports, horse racing is all year round. Kathy Krog: With the jockeys they have to do it so regularly that their eating patterns is what we would term disordered. Up audio: Horses taking off from starting point. V/O Horse racing is one of the most dangerous sports. Every time a jockey gets into the saddle he takes his life in his own hands. Muzi Yeni: So we travel between 55 and close to 65 km an hour. The really top top horses can do 55 seconds over a 1000 metres. So they move. Up audio: Rakeesh in control room rewinding the video on screen and discussing race Rakeesh Jeewanlall: We have emergency services during each running of the race. They follow the field from start to finish so in the event that a horse is broken down and a jockey is dislodged that paramedics are there immediately and our vet is also following the field there to take care of the horse. Anthony Delpech: It is a very dangerous sport. I think I have most probably broken every bone in my body; I have broken my legs; both my collarbones, fractured my skull. I have had my fair share of falls in racing but I think in every sports there is your injury but at the speed we are going, 60, 70 k’s per hour, if you fall at that speed you are going to get hurt. Claire Mawisa: And you still come back for more? Anthony Delpech: Well you have to come back for more. If you feel nervous I think you must hang up your boots because that’s when you won’t be riding your best. You have to just put it behind you and get on with it otherwise you end up losing your nerve which several jockeys I have seen have lost their nerve. V/O Dr Jon Patricios is a Sports Physician in Johannesburg and has been treating jockeys with severe injuries for the past 20 years. Dr Jon Patricios: Sports Physician. Most of the fractures that we see will incur around the shoulder and collarbone area from falls, and similarly we see dislocations in terms of the more severe injuries that is going to cause potential life threatening conditions. Head injuries are top of the list and jockeys suffer more concussions than any other sports. Muzi Yeni: I had one incident where a horse had a heart attack at Greyville. A horse had a heart attack in the middle of a pack but I was fortunate, I only suffered concussion. But I have been fortunate I haven’t broken bones like my colleagues have but a lot of concussion. V/O Concussion accounts for about 20% of jockey injuries; fractures and dislocations another 20% each and less severe injuries the remaining 40%. Dr. Jon Patricios: The difficulty with concussion is there is no visible wound. A jockey who has a headache, has blurred vision, can’t concentrate and has poor balance is a risk to himself and to others. Candice: Delpech: It’s really scary with Anthony out there riding. I only watch him in a race just to make sure he crosses the line safe and sound. Audio up: Anthony at winning post V/O Tonight’s race at the Greyville racecourse ends on a high note for Anthony as he safely crosses the finishing line in first place. Claire Mawisa: Congratulations on your win! Is it still a thrill? Anthony Delpech: Every winner is a thrill. Obviously the bigger ones is more of a thrill but every winner, it is difficult to have a winner, so it is a thrill. V/O The pressure of winning takes its toll on every jockey. The highs and the lows are there every day as they compete in a sport that takes no prisoners. Muzi Yeni: On the race track whether you break a bone or whatever happens you have to be able to get back on that horse the next day because it is your livelihood it is your bread and butter. You got to be able to take the bull by its horns. __________________________________________________________________________ PROMOS AND TEASERS: Sunday teaser: The jockey plays a key role in the highly competitive and glamorous sport of horseracing. We go behind the scenes to find out what they do to stay on top of their game. Before delivery: 30 second visuals unmixed 4-seconds up sound: Muzi Yeni: “If a horse really gets going you can land in the poles.” With delivery mixed: 10 second promo: V/O In this glory filled profession which tempts fate with force and speed, professional jockeys put their lives on the line as they race to the winning post. How do they overcome the dangers? 15 second promo: V/O For jockeys the scale is the enemy. One kilogram over the carded weight and they will be disqualified from the race. Billy Jacobson: For me if I have a light ride coming up I generally won’t eat a day or two before and hot baths and going for a run with sweet clothes on. 15 second promo: V/O Jockeys risk their health and lives to compete in the sport of kings. Anthony Delpech; I think I have most probably broken every bone in my body. In every sport there is your injuries but at the speed we are going 60 kmp if you fall at that speed you are going to get hurt. __________________________________________________________________________ Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for The danger lies (5019) Annalise Lubbe 26 June 2017

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Behind the posh and glamour of horseracing are the lesser known facts about the riders who steer these thoroughbreds. In Carte Blanche tonight we go behind the scenes to tell the story.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Behind the posh and glamour of horseracing are the lesser known facts about the riders who steer these thoroughbreds. In tonight’s episode of Carte Blanche we go behind the scenes and into the jockey’s changeroom on racing day, when shedding the last 500gram in the box (sauna) stands between you and being disqualified. When the scale becomes your enemy and your weight the controlling dial the price you pay to stay in the game takes its toll every step of the way. In the X-games of horses jockeys control half-ton thoroughbreds at neck-breaking speeds, leaving them open to injuries of the worst kind. From broken ribs to collarbones, feet and hands, these are common accidents on the race course every jockey face and those who survive get back into the saddle again. Stamina, capacity for pain, discipline on diet, a challenging lifestyle not cut out for the faint hearted. Jockeys have to have nerves of steel, make split second decisions and never think about the possibility that the beast they steer could stumble and fall, break its leg, tear a tendon, and all that at 60 kilometres per hour with no breaks to put on.
metadata.Summary: Summary: We track a legend who have made history, those who are at the top of their game and the newbie’s; fearless and part of a new generation of jockeys who are invited to compete overseas and taking the challenge. We talk to them and their family about the challenges, their coping mechanisms and how they manage to survive the challenges of weight control, injuries and suspensions - a reality they live with every day.
metadata.Further information: Our story: Bernard Fayd’Herbe wages a constant battle with the scales, as evidenced by the number of times during an afternoon that the commentator announces “plus a half” as he takes his mount down to the start. When he goes on holiday his weight soars from 57kg to as much as 66 kg – “and even at that I still wouldn’t be completely letting myself go. No burgers or anything like that.” Getting the weight down again involves huge willpower. “I have to lose the weight before I exercise. Once you turn the fat into muscle, it can be very hard to get rid of it.” Surprisingly his diet includes three meals a day. He has a cup of black coffee when he gets up and he will have another, or some water, when he is riding work. On returning home he makes himself an omelet. Lunch is fish or steak with salad, and dinner is small, perhaps soup. “You can’t starve yourself. You’ve got to keep healthy but I try to stick to less carbs and low protein.” But the intake has to be paid for and the cost is agonisingly high. He runs a minimum of 10k a day, always in sweat clothes, and on race days he has to sweat again. He reckons a steaming hot bath will shed a kilo and a brisk walk round a racetrack will take off 50% more, assuming the day is sufficiently hot and the clothes heavy enough. At one stage he had to pick and choose his rides on big days because he didn’t have enough energy to ride through the card. There are up to 8 races on a card during competition days. Most jockeys will push their limit and ride all 8 races to maximise their chances of winning. But dehydration and lack of food takes its toll. Rakeesh Jeewanlall, Stipendiary Steward at the Greyville Race Course checks the status of the jockeys before a race and will pull them off if they look too anemic to compete. “Even a glass of water,” he adds, will add too much weight to the jockey so he has to go through the day without any liquid, or go into the box to sweat it out. Garth Puller, former legend Cape jockey with an illustrious career in the saddle and two July wins will tell you that he lived off dried fruit and orange juice for many months, constantly starving himself to maintain the required weight of a professional jockey. This places a great deal of pressure on the jockey to maintain a low body weight, in order to attain rides. Unlike other weight category sports, horseracing does not have an off-season, therefore jockeys are constantly pressured to maintain a below normal body weight. This results in dangerous weight control practices and compromised health. Kathleen Krog, a dietician from Durban recently did a study on apprentice jockeys and found that their micronutrient intakes were 67% below the recommended intake. 91% of the jockeys reported the use of one or more weight control method including skipping meals, excessive exercising to sweat, using the sweatbox (sauna) and in some instances suffering from hunger pains and being over tired. These jockeys are therefore at risk for long-term health consequences including low bone mineral density. Jockeys weigh between 48 and 57 kilograms. The lighter the jockey, the better the horse performs and the faster it goes. On a racecourse the average speed is 60 kilometers per hour. The flip side of being a lightweight jockey means very little control over a beast weighing half a ton and literally running at break necking speeds to the winning post. Justine King has a light frame and is currently the only licensed female jockey in South Africa competes in a male dominant sport. Her life has not been an easy ride and she often have to forfeit a good horse to a male jockey after she has put in the time to train and exercise the animal for a competition. “They just don’t think a girl can do it”, she says. But I am in it and am going to keep on trying to get a win behind my name”. My schooling at the Jockey Academy was tough but the best you can get to get you started,” she exclaims. Laying the foundation for training is the Jockey academy in Summerveld. At 15 years of age applicants are accepted based on their required weight, height and school marks. After five years of skills and academic training those who pass enter the professional arena. Jockeys typically race until they are well in the fifty’s provided they have not suffered from severe lifelong injuries. Retired jockey, Garth accounts one of his several injuries were shortly before race day. “I fracture my wrist and asked the doctor to tie it up. I had to race’. Nowadays they are much more strict. The doctor has to sign you as fit to compete.” Bone fractures and concussion are common injuries. Dr. Jon Patricios, sports physician has treated many jockey injuries at his practice in Johannesburg and found that concussion is often a top cause of falling off the horse at high speeds. The unnatural position of a jockey also accounts for suffering from lower back-pain as thirty one year old Muzi Yeni will tell you. He lives with back pain and is not allowed to take anything stronger than Panado on race days or he will be disqualified. Winning is what it is all about as jockeys get paid a meager R856.50 per race: hardly enough to get out of bed for. Most jockeys are freelancers and will do as many rides a possible on race days to increase their chances to win. Ten percent is the payout for the winning horse and seven percent if you come second, third or fourth. When the stakes are high and everybody wants their share of the payout, no stone will be left unturned. Owners or racehorse trainers will be the first to question the results if they think the jockey has failed to steer the horse in a clear winning position. The National Horseracing Authority governs the sport and any irregularities will be investigated. If the organisation finds that the jockey has been at fault a suspension will be given. South Africa can compete with the best and has produced some of the world’s best jockeys. Anthony Delpech has benefited from gaining international experience and honing his skills in Hong Kong. He has been selected as part of the Rest Of The World Team for the Dubai Duty Free Shergar Cup to be held at Ascot Racecourse in August this year.
